newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Miners' strike, defence sacking row hit Russia.
newsitem.headline: Miners' strike, defence sacking row hit Russia.

text.p: The Kremlin was on Wednesday looking for solutions to a nationwide strike by 400,000 unpaid coalminers and a growing political row over the sacking of the general commanding Russia's land forces.

Trade union officials said 154 out of Russia's 189 pits stopped work on Tuesday when the miners launched a nationwide strike over unpaid wages. They estimated the government owes the miners at least 1.5 trillion roubles ($300 million).
As Kremlin officials struggled to cope with the protest, the defence ministry faced a political scandal.

A commission set up by President Boris Yeltsin to advise him on appointments of top military officials was due to meet on Wednesday amid a row over the defence ministry's dismissal of land forces commander General Vladimir Semyonov.
Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the ministry had jumped the gun and the president had not signed the dismissal decree.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov put off a four-day visit to the United States planned to start on Wednesday although the ministry gave no reason for the postponement.
Miners' leaders called on Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to quit, saying his government was to blame for unpaid wages.
Interfax news agency said Chernomyrdin was likely to fly to Siberia to face the miners on his return from a European security summit that ended in Lisbon on Tuesday.
Interfax quoted Gennady Seleznyov, chairman of the lower house of parliament, as saying after meeting President Boris Yeltsin that Chernomyrdin may fly to the Kuzbass mining region.
Some miners planned an indefinite stoppage, while others were halting deliveries to consumers for 24 or 48 hours. It was not clear how long the actual strike could last.
The miners' pro-democracy and pro-market actions in late 1989 and 1990 helped to undermine the communist regime, fuelling a process that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

But they later turned their anger against new Kremlin rulers as their living standards, once among the highest in the country, nosedived in post-Soviet Russia following economic reforms which led to a steady decline in the mining sector.
The goverment has headed off several major strikes with cash injections and promises of help to restructure the ailing industry.
The defence ministry told the press on Monday that General Semyonov had been sacked "for actions which discredit the honour and dignity of a serviceman and are incompatible with his post".
Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing that Yeltsin had agreed to suspend Semyonov but would not sign his dismissal until the case had been considered by the presidential commission.
Yastrzhembsky said all questions about what he called "this strong formulation" should be addressed to the Defence Ministry. "Somebody was trying to anticipate events," he added.
Semyonov has described charges against him as another attempt to mislead the president and said he had written to Yeltsin to defend himself.
The U.S. embassy in Moscow said it had not yet been informed of the postponement of Rodionov's visit, but a defence ministry spokesman told Reuters that a report by Interfax was correct.
